paper_metadata.title: Continuous-Variable Quantum K-Means Clustering With Photonic Gaussian States

summary: The paper implements a continuous‑variable photonic quantum K‑means algorithm using Gaussian states on the Strawberry Fields/Xanadu platform and evaluates it on IRIS (150 samples), Wine (178), and a synthetic dataset (200). The quantum method achieves clustering accuracy comparable to classical K‑means (e.g., IRIS 88.67% vs 89.33%) and similar SSD values (e.g., IRIS 74.2 vs 78.5) but provides no runtime or complexity advantage.

experiments.description: Continuous-variable quantum K-means clustering on photonic Gaussian states, evaluated on IRIS, Wine, and a synthetic dataset using Strawberry Fields / Xanadu photonic hardware.

algorithm.variant: Continuous-Variable Quantum K-Means (CVQK-Means) with Gaussian states
algorithm.convergence_criteria: repeat assignment/update until centroids converge or maximum iterations reached
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initialize centroids as continuous-variable quantum states; specific initialization method not reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Classical data points are encoded into continuous-variable Gaussian states using displacement and squeezing operations; centroids are also represented as CV quantum states
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize intra-cluster variance / sum of squared distances as in K-means

problem_instance.description: K-means clustering on three datasets: IRIS, Wine, and a synthetic dataset

dataset_specification.description: IRIS (150 instances, 4 features, 3 clusters); Wine (178 instances, 13 features, 3 clusters); Synthetic (200 instances, 5 features, 4 clusters)

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classical data encoded into quadrature variables of Gaussian states; further preprocessing not reported
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compared clustering accuracy and sum of squared distances (SSD) against classical K-means

noise_model.noise_type: quantum noise in photonic hardware (not quantified)

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Encode data into Gaussian states using displacement and squeezing; use beam splitting/interference and homodyne detection for distance estimation
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute clustering accuracy and SSD; compare with classical K-means

speedup_claims.conditions: Empirical comparison on IRIS, Wine, and Synthetic datasets using Strawberry Fields / Xanadu photonic hardware
speedup_claims.caveats: No asymptotic or runtime speedup is reported; the paper only compares clustering accuracy and SSD.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not specified; paper provides no qubit/mode counts, circuit depth, or scaling analysis required to estimate crossover.
limiting_factors: No demonstrated runtime or complexity speedup over classical K-means
No resource reporting (modes, depth, shots, runtime)
Continuous-variable photonic approach not compatible with gate-based quantum computing scope
Classical-to-quantum state preparation via displacement/squeezing may dominate cost
Hardware noise and limited photonic modes discussed as scalability constraints

notes: Paper explicitly states implementation on Xanadu photonic hardware via Strawberry Fields, but does not specify device name, qubit count, circuit depth, shots, or gate counts.
This is continuous-variable photonic quantum computing; the paper does not map the CV system to a discrete qubit register, so num_qubits is not reported.
No asymptotic complexity or speedup claim is given; only empirical comparison to classical K-means.
Tables II and III show nearly identical performance to classical K-means (e.g., IRIS 88.67% vs 89.33% accuracy; Wine 70.22% vs 70.22%).
The paper makes no runtime or complexity advantage claim and reports only comparable clustering quality metrics.
